TWOAT

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
800 AM EDT Sat Sep 26 2026

For the North Atlantic...Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of America:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical
Storm Gonzalo, located just east-northeast of the Cabo Verde
Islands, and on Tropical Depression Fay, located well to the
west-southwest of the Azores.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected during the next 7 days.

$$

The tropical cyclone is clearly still being impacted by both wind shear and dry air. The most recent TAFB Dvorak intensity estimate was T2.0/30 kt, and the objective intensity estimate is in the range of 31-41 kt. Therefore, the initial intensity has been held at 30 kt for this advisory. The cyclone continues to drift towards the west-southwest, at 250/4 kt. A more southerly turn is expected as Fay continues move into the southern flank of the subtropical Atlantic high. By early next week, most of the guidance has the depression turning westward due to the large-scale easterly flow. However there is a bit of uncertainty in the precise timing of this turn. The current NHC forecast track is similar to the previous one with some minor adjustments based on the HCCA forecast aid. There is a high level of uncertainty in the intensity forecast as Fay remains over an area of favorably warm sea-surface temperatures, but vertical wind shear and dry mid-level air will likely continue to hinder the system, preventing a more organized structure from developing. Convection is likely to continue pulsing but the current NHC intensity forecast follows the trend of the previous one showing little change in strength with only minor adjustments made. This forecast continues to maintain Fay as a tropical depression until it becomes post-tropical and dissipates by the middle of next week. DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK ---------------------- At 200 PM CVT (1500 UTC), the center of Tropical Storm Gonzalo was located near latitude 18.8 North, longitude 23.0 West. Gonzalo is moving toward the north-northwest near 10 mph (17 km/h) and this general motion is forecast to continue through the weekend, with a slow down and a turn to the west-northwest anticipated early next week. On the forecast track, the center will continue to move away from northeastern portions of the Cabo Verde Islands today. Maximum sustained winds have decreased to near 40 mph (65 km/h) with higher gusts. Additional weakening is forecast, and Gonzalo is expected to become a remnant low in the next 12-24 hours. Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 185 miles (295 km) from the center. The estimated minimum central pressure is 1005 mb (29.68 inches). HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND ---------------------- SURF: Swells generated by Gonzalo are expected to affect portions of the Cabo Verde Islands through today before diminishing Sunday. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your local weather office. Even though the low-level circulation on GOES-19 visible images appears to be somewhat less elongated than overnight, convection continues to be quite displaced to the northeast due to a brutal 45 kt of southwesterly vertical wind shear. A Metop-C ASCAT pass showed a peak wind of 31 kt to the north of the circulation this morning, but missed the center and the deeper convection to the northeast where the highest winds were previously observed. The initial intensity is thus only lowered to 35 kt this advisory, assuming some stronger winds still exist in the convection to the northeast. The low-level circulation is moving generally north-northwestward at 345 degrees at 9 kt. This general motion should continue today, followed by a slow down and turn to the west-northwest as the increasingly shallow circulation becomes steered by a narrow low-level ridge to its north. The latest NHC track forecast has been shifted slightly further north, following the latest trends in the HFIP Corrected Consensus Approach (HCCA) and Google DeepMind ensemble mean (GDMI) aids. Intensity-wise, Gonzalo likely does not have much time left as a tropical cyclone, with convection becoming increasingly displaced from the center as shear over the system remains above 40 kt. Like the previous forecast, weakening is anticipated, and Gonzalo is forecast to become a remnant low in the next 12 h as the convection is completely stripped away. Total dissipation is likely to occur early next week as the remnant low drifts over the subtropical Eastern Atlantic basin.
